You said:

So, if we make knowledge steward the single writer to the knowledge graph, should we offset that by having the kg-mcp support queries at the deterministic level?

ChatGPT said:

Yes. In fact, those two ideas complement each other.

What you're really doing is separating authority to mutate from authority to observe.

ResponsibilityStewardkg-mcp
Create node✅❌
Modify node✅❌
Merge/supersede concepts✅❌
Classification decisions✅❌
Consistency enforcement✅❌
Deterministic graph queries❌✅
Traversal❌✅
Neighborhood lookup❌✅
Provenance inspection❌✅
Historical reconstruction❌✅

This ends up looking a lot like CQRS:

  • Knowledge Steward = Command side

  • kg-mcp = Query side

The important thing is that kg-mcp should not expose arbitrary graph mutation primitives.

Instead:

Agent
  ↓
kg-mcp.query(...)
  ↓
Graph

Agent
  ↓
KnowledgeSteward.request(...)
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Graph

The deeper question is what you mean by "deterministic level."

I think there are three increasingly powerful query layers.

Level 1: Structural Queries

Pure graph operations.

neighbors(node)
children(node)
parents(node)
path(a,b)

No interpretation.

Just graph mathematics.

Level 2: Ontological Queries

Queries against LOSM semantics.

find WorkRequests
find Classification nodes
find superseded concepts
find active concepts

Still deterministic because they're derived directly from graph state.

Level 3: Derived Reasoning Queries

Computed views.

Why is Conduit classified as a router?

Show evidence.

What changed between April and June?

What classifications conflict?

These are deterministic if implemented as graph algorithms rather than LLM reasoning.

For example:

Explain(concept)

might walk provenance edges and generate:

Conduit
  classified_as ServiceBroker
    evidence: Conversation 17

  reclassified_as EventRouter
    evidence: Conversation 44

  current_state: EventRouter

No model involved.

Just reconstruction.

I would actually push surprisingly far into deterministic territory.

One thing you've repeatedly run into is that LLMs are terrible at faithfully reconstructing history from large contexts.

The graph already knows.

So instead of:

Agent:
Why do we believe Conduit is an Event Router?

the agent should call:

kg-mcp.explain("Conduit")

and receive a deterministic proof chain.

This also aligns with your recent "single writer" thinking.

If Steward becomes the only component allowed to create knowledge:

Transcript
    ↓
Steward
    ↓
Knowledge Graph

then every fact in the graph passed through the same governance process.

At that point kg-mcp can be extremely permissive for reads because reads cannot corrupt state.

In LOSM terms:

Knowledge Steward
    = semantic authority

Knowledge Graph
    = authoritative state

kg-mcp
    = deterministic projection layer

That gives you a very clean invariant:

The graph is never modified through queries, and the graph is never modified except through Steward.

Once that invariant exists, every agent in the ecosystem can query aggressively without risking ontology drift. The graph becomes a shared source of truth, while Steward becomes the sole arbiter of what is allowed to become truth.


You said:

So Steward is the only agent that can write to the KG, but can other processes update it?

ChatGPT said:

I would distinguish between logical writer and physical writer.

If you say:

Steward is the only writer to the KG

that doesn't necessarily mean Steward is the process holding the database connection.

It means:

No state enters the graph without Steward's authorization.

For example:

Transcript
    ↓
Absorb
    ↓
Candidate Knowledge
    ↓
Steward
    ↓ approve
KG Writer
    ↓
Graph

The actual database update might be performed by a repository layer, graph service, event consumer, or transaction manager. Steward remains the semantic authority because it approved the change.

I think there are three possible models.

Model 1: Steward owns every write

Process
   ↓
Steward
   ↓
Graph

Everything routes through Steward.

Advantages:

  • Maximum governance

  • Simple invariant

  • Easy auditing

Disadvantages:

  • Steward becomes a bottleneck

  • Harder to scale

Model 2: Steward approves writes

Process
   ↓
WriteRequest
   ↓
Steward
   ↓ approval
GraphService
   ↓
Graph

This is usually what large systems do.

Steward decides.

Another component executes.

The graph records:

approved_by = Steward
executed_by = GraphService

Model 3: Steward owns ontology, not storage

This is the one I suspect you're drifting toward.

Knowledge Graph
├── Facts
├── Events
├── Provenance
└── Ontology

Steward governs:

Concept creation
Classification
Reclassification
Supersession
Merge
Ontology evolution

But operational processes can write:

ExecutionReceipt
ConversationEvent
ServiceRequest
Telemetry
Observation

directly.

For LOSM, I'd probably split it this way:

Steward owns:
  Concepts
  Classifications
  Relationships
  Canonical Knowledge

Everyone else may write:
  Events
  Observations
  Receipts
  Evidence

Because events are facts that happened.

Ontology is interpretation.

Example:

Vector:
  "Observed Conduit routing 52 requests"

can be written directly.

But:

Conduit IS_A EventRouter

must go through Steward.

That's a very powerful distinction because it separates:

Observation
    ↓
Interpretation
    ↓
Knowledge

which is something you've been converging toward repeatedly in the LOSM discussions.

So my answer would be:

Yes, other processes can update the graph, but only if they are writing observations/evidence. If they are changing the semantic meaning of the graph—concepts, classifications, relationships, ontology—those writes should require Steward authorization.

That keeps Steward from becoming a throughput bottleneck while preserving a single source of semantic truth.
